prompt.context: You're a consultant in 17th century Venice and Powerpoint is your art canvas. Your client, Galileo Galilei, has just invented the telescope. He'd like you to help him make some money off what he is sure will be a very useful invention.
prompt.question: What do you tell him? Help Galileo develop a strategy to commercialize the telescope.

clarifying_info.a: The market being considered is the entire world. Try to derive estimates for specific segments yourself.

clarifying_info.q: What is the population of Italy / Venice / military / traders?
clarifying_info.a: No data is available on that. Why don't you try and derive an estimate for that?

clarifying_info.q: What does it cost to produce a telescope?
clarifying_info.a: Galileo has a workshop and 6 talented workers. Each worker is available 6 days a week for 8 hours a day; all-in labor costs are $10 per worker per hour. Raw materials cost $5 per piece, and one worker can make one telescope in 2 hours.

clarifying_info.q: What skills are needed to make a telescope?
clarifying_info.a: Skills include grinding lenses correctly, building the housing and focal length adjustment mechanism, and assembling the parts.

framework: Company: costs, production capacity, pricing strategy, distribution
Customers: who needs a telescope (local and overseas segments), market sizing, willingness-to-pay
Competitors: threat of imitation, IP risks from workers, obfuscation strategies

questions.prompt: Calculate the cost per unit telescope and weekly production capacity.
questions.guidance: Candidate should explain why cost matters (inform pricing, assess financial resources, compare supply vs demand). Walk through unit cost and then weekly throughput.

math.setup: 6 workers, 6 days/week, 8 hours/day; labor $10/hour; materials $5/unit; 2 hours per telescope
steps: Cost per unit = materials + labor = $5 + (2 hrs × $10/hr) = $25
Weekly worker-hours = 6 workers × 6 days × 8 hrs = 288 worker-hours
math.answer: Unit cost = $25; weekly capacity = 144 telescopes at a total weekly cost of $3,600.

questions.prompt: Who are the key customer segments and what is the largest market at each stage of the product timeline?
questions.guidance: Strong answers categorize by local vs overseas and by use case: traders/sailors, military (army/navy), explorers (land/sea), architects/surveyors. Overseas markets ranked by effort/return: Europe primary, Asia/Middle East/Americas secondary. Candidate should note that large potential demand combined with slow supply suggests premium pricing early on.

questions.prompt: What competitive and IP risks does Galileo face, and how should he address them?
questions.guidance: Key risks: no patent system means imitation is easy; low construction complexity enables reverse-engineering; 6 skilled workers are each an IP risk if they leave. Mitigations: obfuscate the mechanism, keep workers well-compensated and loyal, move fast to build brand and distribution before imitators arrive.

brainstorming.prompt: What distribution strategy should Galileo use and which geographic markets should he prioritize?

categories.name: Local distribution
ideas: Sell directly to local merchants in Venice
Target traders and sailors at the port
Approach the Venetian navy and army directly

categories.name: Overseas distribution
ideas: Partner with overseas trading companies for profit-sharing arrangements
Rank markets by effort vs return: Europe first, Asia/Middle East/Americas later
Consider political considerations in each region

categories.name: Pricing strategy
ideas: Cost-plus pricing based on $25 unit cost
Willingness-to-pay / value-based pricing given monopoly window
Premium pricing while supply is constrained relative to demand

categories.name: Production scaling
ideas: Hire more laborers to increase production capacity beyond 144/week
Weigh additional labor cost vs demand potential
Protect proprietary assembly knowledge when training new workers

recommendation: A large market exists both locally (traders, military, explorers, architects) and overseas (Europe primary, other regions secondary)
Galileo will enjoy a short initial monopoly window; he should price at a premium and scale distribution rapidly before imitators enter
risks: No patent protection means competitors can reverse-engineer the telescope quickly
Skilled workers are IP risks — they could defect and start competing workshops
Local imitators are highly likely given the relatively simple construction
next_steps: Obfuscate the internal mechanism to slow reverse-engineering
Keep all 6 workers well-compensated to reduce defection risk
Build relationships with major trading houses for overseas distribution
Consider hiring additional workers to ramp production and meet initial demand
